To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the pleural cavity is a source of TNF in cancer patients and that TNF is cytotoxic to cancer cells.
the pleural fluid of lung cancer patients contains TNF and that TNF may be involved in the pathophysiology of lung cancer.
the cytotoxic activity in the pleural fluid of a patient with lung adenocarcinoma was identified as TNF by molecular sieving and radioimmunoassays.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the detection of TNF in pleural effusions of lung cancer patients.
the detection and characterization of TNF in pleural effusions of patients with lung carcinoma.
the detection of TNF/cachectin and its activity in the pleural fluid of patients with lung cancers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the pleural fluid of lung cancer patients has a TNF‐like cytotoxic activity against their own lung cancer cells.
TNF is a cytokine that is produced in vivo and has cytotoxicity against tumour cells.
TNF is a cytotoxic factor in carcinomatous pleurisy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
TNF is a pleural effusion factor that has cytotoxic activity in vivo and in vitro against cancer cells.
TNF may play a role in the immunological surveillance against cancer cells.
TNF may be a new therapeutic agent in the treatment of lung cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the pleural fluid of patients with lung cancers may contain a factor with cytotoxic activity against their own cancer cells.
TNF is produced in the pleural cavity in the course of the development of lung cancer.
TNF can be detected in human carcinomatous pleuritis.
